The findings reduce to three coherent corrections: **separate draft visibility from published visibility; remove implicit Card promotion; and use one viewer-owned personal/history projection across working and Library views.** P3 is a consequence of the promotion behaviour, rather than evidence that the persistence coordinator needs redesigning.

This investigation was read-only. I inspected Claude’s probe source and the application call chains; I did not execute tests, change files or connect to a database.

**1. Findings and probe accuracy**

The probes use the real repository and read-model implementations. However, public authoring and Library UI are not exposed in the current private Creator flow, so some probes demonstrate backend defects or superseded backend policies—not currently available browser interactions.

| Finding | Current behaviour | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | `saveDeckDraft(..., "private")` can demote a public Deck immediately. Working access then fails, and one failure aborts `membershipDTO()`. | Genuine backend defect. |
| **P2** | Saving `"public"` changes the Deck root’s access-control visibility before publication. | Genuine exposure bug. |
| **P3** | Public Deck publication promotes private Cards and increments their content revisions. | Real side effect of implicit promotion; removing it resolves this specific stale-lane problem. |
| **P4** | Library-origin forks inherit completion/readings/date, but deliberately exclude reflection/history. | Implements the previous policy; now superseded. |
| **P7** | Working DTO filters chats to the current Deck and does not project inherited history. | Genuine display/projection gap. |
| **P9** | Copy can auto-publish a public destination and consequently expose an owned private Card. | Previous promotion policy must be removed. |
| **P5** | Re-import preserves existing adoption and restores archived membership. | Correct; retain and improve later messaging. |
| **P6** | New entrants receive latest published Cards unless existing CardData already pins another version. | Correct; retain. |
| **P8** | One global personal target date is established through the first relevant opening. | Correct; retain. |

**2. Visibility correction: P1 and P2**

The immediate cause is [saveDeckDraft()](./src/lib/cards/repository.ts:392): it writes `visibility` during draft persistence without a monotonicity check.

The current `/saved` HTTP route does not accept visibility, so ordinary private Creator autosave cannot directly trigger this probe. Nevertheless, the repository boundary is unsafe and would be reused by future public authoring.

Cards have an adjacent problem. [promoteCard()](./src/lib/cards/repository.ts:578) changes published visibility immediately, independently of Card publication. It currently has no application caller, but should not remain as a bypass.

My recommended model is:

- Keep root `visibility` as **effective published access**.
- Add optional draft metadata such as `draftVisibility` for the next publication’s requested visibility.
- Never use draft visibility to authorize non-owner reads.
- Apply the requested visibility only inside successful Card/Deck publication.
- Once effective visibility becomes public, reject requests to make it private.
- Keep unpublished roots inaccessible to foreign users, including roots whose intended first publication is public.

This is actual authoring metadata, not a persisted readiness flag.

Creation helpers that currently accept `"public"` should stage that intention rather than treating an unpublished root as effectively public. Existing published roots retain their stored visibility; there is no automatic content rewrite.

A visibility-only change must count as outstanding publication work. Consequently:

- shared publication rules must compare content **and publication visibility**;
- equal-content saves must retain a draft when visibility is outstanding;
- cancelling a pending promotion should clear the draft if content is also clean;
- publication preparation should replace its current blanket equal-content exception with an explicit visibility-change check;
- recovery must recognize the requested visibility as part of the exact publication outcome.

No historical private-access system is required. This change governs **when** content becomes public and prevents subsequent demotion.

The private first-publication membership exception must use the visibility actually being published. A public first publication must not accidentally create personal membership because the root was private while drafting.

**3. Remove promotion: P3 and P9**

[Public Deck publication](./src/lib/cards/repository.ts:528) currently writes referenced private Card roots and increments their revisions. That entire promotion block should be replaced by validation:

> If the proposed Deck publication is public, every referenced Card must already be effectively public and published.

Owned private Cards may remain in the Deck draft. Their owner must explicitly make them public through successful Card publication before the Deck can publish.

The same predicate should govern:

- publication preparation;
- authoritative Deck publication;
- Copy auto-publication eligibility;
- the Creator blocked-publication explanation.

For Copy into a clean public Deck:

- copying a private Card saves the destination draft;
- the Card remains private;
- no Deck version is created;
- feedback says publication is still required;
- permanent reuse marking still occurs.

Copy into a private Deck may still auto-publish with a private Card when the other requirements pass.

**P3 confirmation:** removing implicit promotion removes the Card content-revision increment that the probe detects. Existing reference bookkeeping changes `referenceRevision`/reuse metadata, not the Card autosave revision. I recommend an actual coordinator regression test to prove this, but no special reconciliation machinery.

Explicit publication of the Card itself remains a legitimate revision-changing operation and must return its normal acknowledgement.

Copy recovery must retain its existing exact-outcome behaviour: a later explicit Card promotion must not cause a retry of an earlier draft-only Copy to reinterpret itself as auto-publication.

**4. Uniform fork carryover: P4**

The existing relationship is a suitable foundation. The problem is the origin gate in [inheritForkCardData()](./src/lib/cards/forks.ts:67).

Remove that gate for personal Card continuity. Whenever the publishing actor has eligible immediate-source CardData:

- copy completion/skipped, readings, target date and reflection once;
- establish `historySourceCardTemplateId`;
- leave chats, tests and media stored on their source records;
- leave source CardData unchanged.

Everything remains inside the first successful Card-publication transaction.

Retain:

- exact immutable canonical fork source;
- validated immediate Step lineage;
- defensive identity intersection;
- coherent publication-time source snapshot;
- no personal records at fork autosave;
- no inheritance replay on later publication or retry.

`ForkContext` still serves other purposes: source-view authorization and Deck cadence/navigation continuity. It should no longer decide whether the actor’s Card reflection/history carries.

All personal relationships remain inside the actor’s User document. Publishing canonical content must not serialize that personal layer into a public version or public response.

Already completed v1 recovery must remain read-only. Old disposable forks created under the previous policy should not acquire refreshed state merely by retrying publication.

**5. Working/history display: P7**

Two separate gaps exist in [projectWorking()](./src/lib/cards/readModels.ts:38):

- chats are filtered by the newly opened Deck ID;
- only the target CardData’s media/reflection are projected; inherited segments are not consumed.

Additionally, tests are absent from the working DTO/`WeeklyCard` interface, and there is no existing test-results renderer.

The smallest coherent correction is a shared, actor-owned Card personal projection used by working views, membership display and later personalized Library views:

- current-state fields come from the current CardData;
- historical segments come from `personalHistorySegments()`;
- unchanged Cards use their existing global CardData, including original-context chats;
- forked Cards include their source chain;
- original Card and chat Deck context remain attached;
- segments are not copied into persistence arrays.

I recommend keeping **current writable records separate from read-only historical segments**. Rendering may combine their visible artifacts, but mutation code must retain the original source identity.

This matters particularly for media:

- inherited media must not be submitted as new uploads;
- a delete action must not accidentally address the target Card instead of the source;
- optimistic current-media updates must not erase displayed inherited media.

Affected frontend areas include `cardLayout.ts`, `FocusedCardView.tsx`, `DeckDetail.tsx` and `workingCardStore.ts`. Render identities should include source context where event IDs alone could collide.

The history endpoint’s explicit `currentAdoptedCardTemplateVersion` and `eventVersionAttribution: "not-recorded"` distinction should remain unchanged.

**6. Library personal layer and preserved adoption**

`resolveDeckPreview()` currently intentionally supplies no personal records. That remains useful as a **canonical-only resolver**, but is insufficient as the final Library presentation.

Phase 4 should compose canonical content with only the authenticated viewer’s own personal projection:

- anonymous viewers receive canonical content;
- authenticated viewers may receive their own existing CardData/history;
- viewing creates no personal records;
- neither author ownership nor provenance selects whose personal records are returned;
- personalized responses must not enter shared public caches.

Public DTOs should explicitly exclude draft metadata and personal fork context rather than spreading entire roots into responses.

P5 and P6 already match the requirements:

- `ensureDeckData()` preserves existing Deck adoption and reactivates archived membership;
- `ensureCompositionCardData()` preserves existing Card adoption;
- missing CardData adopts the Card root’s latest published version;
- historical resolution uses `cardVersionAtPublish`;
- working resolution uses personal adoption.

Keep these mechanics. Add the Phase 4/5 upfront explanation that existing adoption is retained and an Update is available.

P8 needs no change.

**7. My Decks resilience**

Enforcing permanent public visibility is the primary fix. Separately, `membershipDTO()` currently throws for a single inaccessible/malformed entry, including through the actual `/decks` page.

I recommend preserving batched queries but isolating known content-resolution failures per membership. Return an explicit unavailable entry with safe personal identifiers and an error code, while allowing valid Decks to render.

Do not delete membership, silently hide it, or swallow authentication/database failures. This needs a small unavailable-entry presentation in the My Decks caller; it is not a replacement for visibility enforcement.

**8. Implementation order and regression tests**

I would implement this in four reviewable changes:

| Change | Main files | Essential coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Visibility lifecycle | `model.ts`, `publicationRules.ts`, repository and canonical endpoints | No demotion; staging does not expose content; failed publication leaves access unchanged; visibility-only publication |
| Public-reference validation | Repository publication/Copy paths and presentation rules | Private Card blocks public publication; Copy remains draft-only; no Card revision bump; exact retry recovery |
| Uniform personal continuity | `forks.ts`, repository, history tests | Library/My Decks carry the same eligible state; no-source case; actor isolation; coherent snapshot; no re-inheritance |
| History projection/display and resilience | Read models, Card types/layout/components/cache, My Decks callers | Original-context chats visible; inherited artifacts visible once; mutation targeting preserved; one bad membership does not break others |

Tests requiring replacement or adjustment:

- `zz-review-probes.integration.ts`: its passing assertions currently preserve the unwanted behaviours. Replace them with desired-behaviour regressions.
- `card-foundation.integration.ts`: replace the automatic-promotion expectation.
- `creator-lifecycle.integration.ts`: preserve visibility-only publication coverage using staged visibility and explicitly public Cards.
- `card-forks.test.ts` and `card-forks.integration.ts`: replace Library-origin reflection/history exclusion expectations.
- Keep Library-with-no-source-CardData tests.
- Extend Copy tests for public/private combinations and a coordinator save immediately after Deck publication.
- Add working DTO **and rendered UI** history assertions; endpoint-only tests do not prove display.
- Retain P5/P6/P8 as positive regression tests with corrected descriptions.

After implementation, run the established full unit/integration/E2E/Phase 2 browser/typecheck/lint/build/diff verification.

No production migration is needed for this correction. Optional draft metadata can support existing roots without rewriting immutable content. The migration validator already rejects private Cards in public Decks and should retain that invariant.

**9. QUESTION FOR USER**

Three decisions remain for complete Library/display implementation; they do not block the visibility or carryover corrections.

**Library canonical version**

If CardData adopts v1 but the latest public Card is v3, which should the personalized Library initially display?

- Adopted v1, with an explicit latest preview/Update path.
- Latest v3, overlaying applicable personal state by stable Step identity.

I recommend adopted v1 by default when personal data exists, while retaining explicit latest preview. Your existing exact-viewed-version fork rule supports either choice.

**Library personal editing**

Does “normal Card UI” include editing existing personal state from Library, or displaying it only?

Current personal mutation/upload authorization requires an active working Deck context. Library viewing may have CardData without any active Deck membership.

If editing is intended, I recommend a separately validated personal Card boundary based on authenticated data ownership and adopted content—not weakening the existing working-Deck checks implicitly.

**Test-history placement**

There is no existing test-results surface to reconnect. Where should those retained results appear?

I recommend a small read-only history area in the existing focused Card view, preserving source context and avoiding Progress/counting semantics. Backend-only exposure would not satisfy the requirement that results are actually displayed.

Phases 6–7 should consume this same contextual history model rather than introducing physical copies or counting the same source events independently through each descendant.

> \- chats\
> \- tests\
> \- personal media\
> \
> Instead:\
> \- keep those records stored on their original source CardData/context;\
> \- establish/use the personal history/source relationship so they remain visible on the forked Card;\
> \- preserve original Card/Deck/event context;\
> \- source CardData remains unchanged;\
> \- no later re-inheritance or replay.\
> \
> If the user has no source CardData, there is naturally nothing personal to inherit.\
> \
> This must behave the same whether the fork was initiated from Library or My Decks.\
> \
> All of this personal data/history is private to that user and must never leak into canonical public content or to other Library users.\
> \
> \## 4. P7 / history projection — implement\
> \
> Fix the current gap where chats/tests/media can disappear when viewing a continued/forked Card from an adapted Deck.\
> \
> Desired behaviour:\
> \- chats/tests/media remain stored once in their original context;\
> \- they are NOT duplicated or reassigned;\
> \- they ARE displayed on the continued/forked Card through the personal source/history chain.\
> \
> Use one coherent viewer-owned personal/history projection rather than different behaviour for working vs forked views.\
> \
> Please preserve mutation correctness:\
> \- inherited media must not be treated as new uploads;\
> \- delete/update actions must target the original source record;\
> \- current writable state and read-only historical segments should remain distinguishable internally even if rendered together.\
> \
> \## 5. Library behaviour — revise from your previous recommendation\
> \
> We have changed the product decision here.\
> \
> The Library should NOT overlay the user’s personal CardData onto Library Cards.\
> \
> Reason:\
> \- Library represents the latest public canonical content;\
> \- the user may still be using an older adopted version in My Decks;\
> \- overlaying old personal state onto newer Library content would be misleading.\
> \
> So:\
> \
> Library = canonical public content only.\
> \
> If the current user already has that Deck/Card in their personal collection:\
> \- show a clear status such as already imported / in My Decks / archived / update available;\
> \- the item may be visually muted if useful;\
> \- buttons should change appropriately, e.g. Open / Restore / Update available rather than Import/Get Started.\
> \
> Do NOT show in the Library view:\
> \- completion\
> \- signals\
> \- reflection\
> \- target date\
> \- chats\
> \- tests\
> \- personal media\
> \
> Those belong to the user’s working/My Decks experience.\
> \
> Viewing Library content must create no personal records.\
> \
> Keep Library canonical resolution separate from personal adopted-version resolution.\
> \
> \## 6. P5 — preserve current behaviour\
> \
> Do not silently upgrade existing personal adoption.\
> \
> If a user restores an archived Deck:\
> \- restore/unarchive the existing DeckData/version/state;\
> \- do not silently advance to latest;\
> \- later show Update available.\
> \
> If another imported Deck contains a Card for which the user already has older CardData:\
> \- keep their existing adopted Card version;\
> \- later show Card Update available.\
> \
> Add/retain the information needed so the UI can clearly explain this later.\
> \
> \## 7. P6 — preserve current behaviour\
> \
> Do not change new-user Card adoption to the Deck’s historical \`cardVersionAtPublish\`.\
> \
> Intended rule:\
> \- Deck version records the Card version that existed when the Deck was published;\
> \- existing users stay on their adopted Card version until explicit Update;\
> \- a brand-new user entering the Deck gets the Card root’s latest published version, unless they already have CardData for that Card;\
> \- Bob publishing Card v2 does not mutate Alice’s immutable Deck version.\
> \
> Please keep regression coverage for this.\
> \
> \## 8. P8 — no change\
> \
> One personal target date per Card.\
> \
> The first relevant Deck opening/cadence calculation may establish it.\
> \
> Do not introduce per-Deck target dates.\

> - do not change the Card header or build the modal unless one already exists and a tiny wiring change is genuinely necessary for regression correctness.

> ```

> \## 10. My Decks resilience\
> \
> I agree that one bad/inaccessible membership should not crash the entire My Decks response.\
> \
> Please harden this.\
> \
> However:\
> \- do not delete membership;\
> \- do not silently hide it as the primary fix;\
> \- do not use this as a substitute for enforcing visibility invariants.\
> \
> If an explicit unavailable entry is the cleanest backend/read-model representation, implement that foundation, but keep the exact final UI treatment minimal and non-prescriptive unless required.\

Implemented the corrections. Full verification is green.

1. **What changed**
   - Card/Deck visibility changes remain draft intent until successful publication. Published public content cannot become private.
   - Public Deck publication rejects private Cards. Copying a private Card into a public Deck saves draft-only, preserves privacy and supports exact retry recovery.
   - Removed implicit Card promotion and its Card-revision bump, eliminating P3’s cause.
   - Fork publication now uniformly carries the viewer’s completion/skipped, readings, reflection and target date.
   - Chats/tests/media remain source-stored and accessible through viewer-owned history. Working UI displays retained observations/media; inherited media stays read-only in the fork’s upload editor.
   - Library preview remains canonical-only.
   - My Decks retains explicit unavailable entries alongside valid Decks and exposes update-availability metadata.
   - P5/P6/P8 adoption/date behaviour remains intact.

2. **Implementation adjustments**
   - Added separate `draftVisibility` intent and immutable-version visibility metadata for publication/recovery checks.
   - Reused the existing personal-history relationship and shared projection. No special P3 coordinator reconciliation was needed.

3. **Remaining concerns**
   - Existing published forks are not backfilled or re-inherited.
   - Test-history UI remains deferred; complete context-preserving data is exposed.
   - Six existing lint warnings remain unchanged. No new warnings or errors.

> Please read Claude’s final review (at the bottom under the title CLAUDES REVIEW, but treat the product decisions written here above the CLAUDE REPORT as authoritative wherever they differ from Claude’s interpretation.
>
> Do not let Claude’s wording steer the implementation away from these decisions. Some of Claude’s findings are valid defects; others describe intentional behaviour or misunderstand our architecture.
>
> Please first inspect the relevant code and then implement the required corrections. Use your own judgment for the technical approach. If there is a safer/cleaner implementation than Claude’s suggested mitigation, use it and explain why.
>
> ## Important correction to Claude’s P6 statement
>
> Claude’s final report says:
>
> > “Adoption now correctly pins to the cardVersionAtPublish stored in the Deck…”
>
> That is NOT our intended behaviour.
>
> Preserve the existing rule:
>
> - `cardVersionAtPublish` records the Card version that existed when that Deck version was published.
> - It is historical/provenance information.
> - Existing users stay on the Card version already in their CardData until explicit Update.
> - A new user entering a Deck adopts the latest published version of each Card, unless they already have CardData for that Card at another version.
> - Publishing a newer Card version does NOT mutate the immutable Deck version.
> - Do not change this behaviour in response to Claude’s report.
>
> ## R1 — private-era Card versions must remain private
>
> Claude is correct that this is a real privacy issue.
>
> Firm rule:
>
> - Making a Card public now must NOT retrospectively expose versions that were created/published while the Card was private.
> - A non-owner may only view/fork a specific Card version if that specific version was public.
> - A public current Card root is not sufficient authorization to access all historical versions.
> - The owner may of course retain access to their own private historical versions.
>
> Please apply this consistently to Library preview, exact-version viewing, fork creation and any other foreign-access path.
>
> This must be fixed before public Library use.
>
> ## R2 — personal CardData media deletion through Card forks
>
> Be precise here: this concerns ONLY user-uploaded personal media stored in `CardData`.
>
> It does NOT concern canonical/template media such as:
> - Card intro image/video;
> - Step instructional image/video;
> - any media belonging to `CardTemplate` content.
>
> Scenario:
>
> - Alice has personal CardData for source Card A.
> - Alice uploaded her own personal image/video to that CardData.
> - Alice later creates Card fork B.
> - B does not physically copy Alice’s personal upload.
> - B displays that source-stored upload through Alice’s personal-history relationship.
> - The source Deck may later be archived or otherwise no longer active.
>
> Firm rule:
>
> - Alice must still be able to delete HER underlying personal media item while viewing it through B.
> - Deletion targets the original source CardData/media record.
> - It is one underlying media item, so deleting it removes it everywhere Alice’s personal-history projection would otherwise show it:
>   - source Card;
>   - descendant fork(s);
>   - any other personal view projecting that same item.
> - Do NOT introduce fork-specific “hide this media here only” behaviour for v1.
> - Do NOT duplicate the media into descendant CardData merely to make deletion easier.
>
> Security requirement:
>
> Do NOT simply remove authorization checks globally.
>
> The desired outcome is:
>
> > The authenticated user who owns the CardData/media item may manage/delete their own personal upload even if the source Card is no longer reachable through an active Deck.
>
> Other users must remain unable to mutate it.
>
> Canonical/template media permissions remain completely separate.
>
> Please design the safest authorization boundary that achieves that rule.
>
> ## R3 — malformed personal history must fail gracefully
>
> Claude is correct.
>
> Firm user-facing rule:
>
> - A malformed historical chat/test/media/history item must never make the user’s current Card or entire Deck unusable.
> - One corrupt source-history record must not cascade into several descendant Decks becoming unavailable.
> - Preserve as much valid history as possible.
> - If an individual history item cannot be interpreted safely, isolate that item rather than failing the whole Card/Deck experience.
> - Do not hide authentication/authorization/database failures under this rule; this is about malformed personal-history data.
>
> Fix before continuing.
>
> ## R4 — sibling forks showing the same history is intentional
>
> Claude labels this “duplicated history on sibling forks”.
>
> Do NOT treat this as a defect.
>
> Example:
>
> A -> B
> A -> C
>
> If B and C are both descendants of A for the same user, then both may legitimately display A’s historical:
> - chats;
> - tests;
> - personal CardData media.
>
> The records are not duplicated in storage. They are being projected through two valid ancestry relationships.
>
> That is intended.
>
> Do not deduplicate them globally merely because sibling descendants display the same source history.
>
> ### Later UX TODO — do not solve now
>
> Add this to the deferred product/UX list:
>
> Multiple Deck/Card adaptations could become confusing even when the underlying history model is correct.
>
> Later we should review how to:
> - help users identify which programme is their current one;
> - encourage/archive superseded Decks where appropriate;
> - avoid accidentally continuing a chat in an old programme context;
> - manage several successive forks/adaptations without exposing technical fork-tree complexity;
> - potentially offer a future choice such as “keep both” vs “replace/archive old programme”.
>
> Do NOT automatically archive original Decks now unless an existing rule already requires it.
>
> ## R5 — CardData without current Deck membership is intentional
>
> Claude calls this “orphan personal state”.
>
> Do NOT treat it as a defect or cleanup target.
>
> Firm architecture rule:
>
> `CardData` means the user has personal learning state associated with that Card identity.
>
> It does NOT mean that the Card must currently belong to an active Deck in My Decks.
>
> CardData must be allowed to survive:
> - Deck archive;
> - Card removal from a Deck;
> - temporary lack of any active Deck reference;
> - Library/fork workflows;
> - future standalone Card workflows.
>
> One reason we deliberately retain it is that if the user later encounters/imports that Card again, their previous learning state is still available.
>
> Do not delete or suppress CardData merely because no current Deck membership references it.
>
> ## R6 — inherited target date is intentional
>
> Claude recommends clearing/recalculating the inherited target date when a fork enters a new Deck.
>
> Do NOT do that.
>
> Firm rule:
>
> When eligible personal state is carried from source CardData to a Card fork, carry:
> - completion/skipped;
> - signals;
> - reflection;
> - target date.
>
> The target date represents that user’s existing commitment/state for the continuing Card journey.
>
> If the new Card later appears in another Deck, its inherited personal target date takes precedence over generated Deck cadence.
>
> There remains ONE personal target date per CardData.
>
> Do not introduce per-Deck target dates.
>
> Do not silently replace an inherited target date because the fork is inserted into a Deck with a different cadence.
>
> The user may change their target date explicitly later.
>
> ## Multi-fork chains — intended recursive history
>
> Claude raises:
>
> A -> B -> C
>
> Firm rule:
>
> C should be able to surface the relevant personal-history ancestry from both:
> - B;
> - A.
>
> This recursive history is intentional.
>
> There is no product-level maximum fork depth.
>
> Do not truncate legitimate finite chains merely because several generations exist.
>
> The UI should hide the technical ancestry complexity from the user and simply show relevant history naturally.
>
> Technical cycle/corruption protection is still required:
> - corrupted cycles must not recurse forever;
> - repeated segments/events should not appear accidentally more than intended;
> - legitimate long finite chains remain valid.
>
> ## Claude’s Deck-update concern — product clarification
>
> Claude worries about source Cards being radically changed/replaced and history becoming confusing.
>
> The intended product model significantly limits this concern.
>
> A Card should remain fundamentally the same learning concept across versions.
>
> Normal same-Card evolution may include:
> - wording improvements;
> - video changes;
> - Step refinement;
> - reasonable evolution of the same learning objective.
>
> If the meaning/objective changes substantially, creators should create a NEW Card.
>
> Example:
>
> Changing a Card from “Finishing” into “Creating chances” should normally be a new Card, not a radically changed version of the same Card.
>
> Fundamental programme changes therefore happen at Deck level by:
> - adding Cards;
> - removing Cards;
> - replacing Cards;
> - reordering Cards.
>
> A user’s existing Deck fork remains based on the exact earlier Deck version they forked. Later upstream Deck changes do not rewrite their fork.
>
> Do not design a complex Card semantic-merge system to solve a product behaviour we do not intend to support.
>
> Later we may add guidance/warnings for creators making extremely large Card changes, but that is not part of this task.
>
> ## Phase 5 cross-owner editing — preserve the user experience requirement
>
> Claude’s technical concern about the persistence coordinator may be valid and should be investigated during Phase 5.
>
> The firm user-facing rule is:
>
> Editing another user’s content should feel like one continuous edit.
>
> When Alice edits Bob’s Card:
> - she presses Edit;
> - the first meaningful persisted change internally creates her owned fork;
> - editing continues seamlessly;
> - she should not lose keystrokes or edits;
> - she should not see duplicate Cards appear;
> - she should not need to reload;
> - she should not experience a visible technical identity transition;
> - pending/in-flight work must not become attached to the wrong Card.
>
> The exact coordinator/handoff implementation is for you to design during Phase 5.
>
> Do not prematurely implement Phase 5 here unless a foundational correction is required now.
>
> ## Existing fork personal-state rule remains
>
> For clarity, retain the rule already agreed after Claude’s first review:
>
> If the FORKING USER has eligible source CardData, first publication of the Card fork copies once:
> - completion/skipped;
> - signal readings;
> - reflection;
> - target date.
>
> It does NOT physically copy:
> - chats;
> - tests;
> - personal CardData media.
>
> Those remain stored in source CardData and are surfaced through the viewer-owned personal-history relationship.
>
> This behaviour is the same whether the fork was initiated from Library or My Decks.
>
> If the user has no source CardData, there is nothing personal to inherit.
>
> Personal history is always scoped to the authenticated user and must never leak through public canonical Card/Deck content to another user.
>
> ## Library remains canonical-only
>
> Do not revert our Library decision.
>
> Library shows the latest public canonical content only.
>
> It does NOT overlay the viewer’s:
> - progress;
> - signals;
> - reflection;
> - target date;
> - chats;
> - tests;
> - personal CardData media.
>
> If the viewer already has that Card/Deck in their personal collection, Library should later show status/action differences such as:
> - already imported;
> - Open;
> - Restore;
> - Update available.
>
> But the Library content itself remains canonical-only.
>
> ## Test-history UI remains deferred
>
> Do not invent a new test-history UI during these fixes.
>
> Intended later UI:
> - Card header shows latest three test-result indicators;
> - clicking them opens the full test-history modal;
> - modal shows the complete test history;
> - same modal can later be reused from Progress.
>
> For now, preserve/expose the complete context-correct history data required by that future UI.
>

> CLAUDES REPORT
>
> Based on the Codex technical report, the product context (early-stage startup, v1 product, small trial), and multiple rounds of active integration testing (probes), here is the final critical review of the Phase 1-3 architecture and its readiness for Phases 4-7.
> Codex has successfully addressed the primary P1-P9 visibility and lifecycle flaws. The architecture now correctly enforces:
> - Draft vs. Effective Visibility: Visibility changes are properly deferred until publication. Saving drafts no longer prematurely alters root visibility.
> - Monotonic Visibility: The transition of states prevents silent breakages for followers.
> - Safe Forwards/Adoption Pinning: Adoption now correctly pins to the cardVersionAtPublish stored in the Deck rather than floating to latestVersion, ensuring curated cohorts receive stable content.
> - The Core Split: The separation between CardTemplate (canonical) and CardData (personal learning state) remains a robust and correct foundation.
> The introduction of the personal-history projection and library forks solved earlier issues but introduced new edge cases. I ran 6 additional probe tests (R1-R6) against the updated logic. All tests passed, confirming the following behaviors exist in the codebase today.
> CAUTION
>  Most Serious Risks (Fix Before Next Phase) These issues directly cause data leaks, application crashes, or severe UX blockers.
> - R1: Privacy Leak via Version Promotion A non-owner can fork a private-era version of a Card if the Card was later promoted to public. The system records version visibility but does not enforce it during library forks, exposing historical private data.
> - R3: Brittle History Projection (Crash Cascade) The new history projection is extremely brittle. A single malformed history record (e.g., a hand-repaired date string instead of an object) on a source CardData crashes the projection. This causes every Deck containing the fork to throw INVALID_PERSONAL_HISTORY and become "Unavailable", locking the user out of multiple programs simultaneously.
> - Phase 5 Risk - Coordinator Identity Transition The CreatorPersistenceCoordinator tightly binds active editing lanes to cardTemplateId. In Phase 5 (Foreign Edit), editing a foreign card causes a fork (generating a new cardTemplateId). The coordinator currently lacks a mechanism to seamlessly transition the in-flight lane to this new identity, risking detached edits, lost data, or application crashes.
> WARNING
>  Curation & UX Risks (Should Fix) These create confusing user experiences and block basic content management.
> - R2: Orphaned Read-Only Media Inherited media is displayed on a fork but cannot be deleted by the user. Media mutators require the source Card to be in an active working Deck. If the source Deck is archived (or not active), the user is permanently stuck with media they cannot remove from their new fork.
> - R6: Inherited Target Dates Override Cadence When a user forks a card, it inherits the old targetDate. If they add this fork to a new Deck with its own cadence, the old inherited date overrides the new Deck's cadence. This breaks the expected scheduling of the new curriculum.
> NOTE
>  Reasonable Trade-offs (Acceptable for v1) Given the scale of the v1 trial, these are acceptable quirks to document and leave as-is to save engineering time.
> - R4: Duplicated History on Sibling Forks Sibling forks of the same source duplicate the history projection (both show the exact same source media/chats). Given the scale of v1, this visual duplication is acceptable.
> - R5: Orphan Personal State Canonical-only/Library forks create personal CardData without a corresponding membership record. While slightly untidy ("orphan" state), it does not break functionality.
> As we move into Phase 4 (Public Library), Phase 5 (Cross-Owner Editing), and Phase 7 (Updates), be aware of the following:
> - Deck Updates & History Inheritance: When a Deck is updated to a new version, how does the personal-history projection handle Cards that were swapped or heavily modified? If a user forks a Card that was later replaced in the upstream Deck, ensure their history does not detach or become confusing.
> - Multi-fork Chains: The current history projection works for a single fork. If a user forks a fork (A -> B -> C), does C inherit A's history? Ensure the projection doesn't infinitely recurse or drop context unexpectedly.
> 1. Enforce Version Visibility (R1): Add a strict visibility check in the libraryFork or fork creation command to ensure the requested version was public at the time of creation, not just that the Card root is currently public.
> 2. Harden the History Projection (R3): The projection mapping must fail gracefully. If a record is malformed, log the error and omit that single record or provide a graceful fallback, rather than throwing a hard error that brings down the entire Deck context.
> 3. Decouple Media Deletion from Active Source Decks (R2): Allow media mutators to delete media on the fork if it was inherited, perhaps by soft-deleting or overriding the inherited array on the fork's CardData, without requiring the source to be active.
> 4. Target Date Recalculation (R6): When a forked Card is added to a new Deck, explicitly recalculate or clear the inherited targetDate so it respects the new Deck's cadence.
> 5. Phase 5 Coordinator Handoff: Before starting Phase 5, design a "Lane Identity Handoff" protocol for the CreatorPersistenceCoordinator. When a fork occurs during an edit, the backend must return the new cardTemplateId and the coordinator must hot-swap the lane ID without dropping in-flight edits.
> Overall, the architecture is moving in the right direction, and the fixes for P1-P9 are solid. These new specific boundaries between immutable canonical history and mutable personal state require hardening before exposing them to the trial group.

Implemented R1–R3. No product behaviour was changed for R4–R6 or P5/P6/P8.

- **R1:** Foreign reads and forks now require the requested immutable Card version to be public. This covers preview, historical/working resolution, adoption and update notes. Owners retain historical access. Versions without recorded visibility fail closed for foreign access.
- **R2:** Personal-media deletion now authorizes against the authenticated user’s own CardData and deletes the original source item. The existing media editor supports inherited items, including when the source Deck is archived. Personal video-status checks use the same ownership principle. Upload and canonical-media permissions remain separate.
- **R3:** History projection isolates malformed items, preserves valid history and safely handles corrupt cycles. Legitimate finite chains have no depth limit. Authentication and database failures remain errors.

Claude’s **R4 sibling history, R5 retained CardData and R6 inherited dates are intentional** and remain intact. New entrants still adopt the latest published Card version unless existing CardData already pins another version; `cardVersionAtPublish` remains historical information.

The round-two probes became permanent regressions in [card-review-regressions.integration.ts](./tests/card-review-regressions.integration.ts). Added unit and browser coverage verifies authorization, source deletion, malformed history and navigation waiting for deletion. Deferred adaptation guidance is recorded in [outstanding-tasks.md](./docs/design/outstanding-tasks.md).

**QUESTION FOR USER — private-era Deck history**

An adjacent gap remains: after a private Deck becomes public, exact-version access can expose its earlier private title/introduction where its Cards were public. Should private-era **Deck versions** also become owner-only for viewing and forking? I recommend applying the same version-level protection. I left this unchanged pending your decision.

Phase 5’s seamless editing-identity handoff remains deferred; no foreign-edit UI was introduced.

> Yes — please apply the same version-level privacy rule to Decks.
>
> Firm rule:
>
> - If a Deck version was private when it was published, that specific immutable version remains private permanently.
> - Making a later Deck version public must NOT retrospectively expose earlier private-era Deck versions.
> - Foreign users must not be able to view or fork those earlier private versions, even if all referenced Cards happen to be public.
> - The owner retains access to their own private historical versions.
> - If an older Deck version lacks enough visibility metadata to prove it was public, fail closed for foreign access.
>
> Please implement the smallest coherent equivalent of the Card version-level protection, add regression coverage, run the usual verification, and report the result.

> Go back over your plan for phase 4 given the changes and product decisions that have been made since you last produced it. Tighten up the plan and report back to me with the detailed implementation plan. Make sure to include all likely Edge cases and risks. Make sure to come back to me with any questions rather than making your own mind up about implementation decisions that have an impact on user experience in any way even the smallest way. I want to have my eyes over every decision that I fix how the app works in terms of its functionality and it's user experience. You are free to plan the implementation of these technically. Highlight any aspects of the plan that you are particularly keen to have a second opinion on because you were torn between different approaches.
>
> To help you here is my current understanding of events guided by another chat I am in with ChatGPT. Where any of this contradicts your understanding do not accept what I am saying but challenge me instead by raising it as an issue for us to discuss.
>
> Here it is:
> My understanding of Phase 4 is that this is the first phase where the architecture we have built becomes a genuine public-content workflow rather than primarily a creator/personal-data architecture.
> At a high level, Phase 4 should let one user publish a Deck publicly, let another user encounter that Deck in a minimal Library experience, inspect it without creating personal state, and then deliberately bring it into My Decks.
> I would frame Phase 4 as having four user-facing pieces.
> 1. A creator can publish a Deck for other users
> The creator already has the canonical Card/Deck draft and publication machinery from Phases 1–3. Phase 4 should expose the minimum public publication experience necessary for another user to consume it.
> The important rules we have already settled are:
> - A Deck may be private or public while being drafted.
> - Draft visibility is only draft intent; changing a draft to public must not expose anything until publication succeeds.
> - Once a Deck has actually been publicly published, it cannot later become private.
> - A public Deck may contain only public Cards.
> - Publishing a public Deck must therefore be blocked if any referenced Card is private.
> - The system must never automatically make a private Card public merely because somebody is publishing a public Deck.
> - A private Deck is perfectly allowed to use public Cards.
> - Public/private status belongs to the immutable versions too. Publishing Deck v4 publicly does not expose private-era v1–v3.
> So from the creator's point of view I envisage something roughly like:
> Finish Deck → choose/public visibility → Publish
>
> and if a referenced Card is still private:
> “This Deck can't be published publicly because Card X is private.”
>
> The creator then explicitly publishes that Card if that is what they want. We should not silently solve it for them.
> I don't think Phase 4 needs sophisticated publishing management, discovery metadata, moderation workflows or audience controls. It needs the smallest trustworthy path from a valid canonical draft to publicly consumable content.
> 2. A user can browse/preview public content in a Library
> This is deliberately a minimal Library, not the full Library/discovery product planned for Phase 7.
> Its job is essentially to prove the public consumption boundary:
> “Here is public canonical content that exists independently of my personal learning state.”
>
> That distinction is important.
> When Alice looks at Bob's Deck in the Library, she should see the public canonical Deck and its public canonical Cards.
> She should not see the Library Deck transformed by her own personal data.
> So Library preview should not overlay:
> - Alice's completion;
> - skipped status;
> - signal readings;
> - reflection;
> - target dates;
> - personal uploads;
> - chats;
> - tests.
> That remains true even if Alice already has the same Card in one of her own Decks.
> This was one of the important conclusions from the review because otherwise the Library becomes conceptually muddled: Bob's latest public Card might be v4 while Alice's personal CardData might deliberately still be on v2.
> The Library therefore answers:
> What is publicly available now?
>
> My Decks answers:
> What version am I personally using, and what have I done with it?
>
> Those are intentionally separate views.
> Which versions does the Library show?
> My understanding is:
> - Library presents the latest public canonical Deck version.
> - Within that public Deck, the preview should resolve the public canonical Card content appropriate to the Library rather than Alice's adopted personal versions.
> - Private historical Deck/Card versions remain inaccessible to foreign users.
> - Missing historical visibility metadata fails closed.
> I would expect us to make this version resolution very explicit with Codex before implementation because we have deliberately separated historical cardVersionAtPublish, latest canonical public Card, and the version Alice has adopted personally.
> 3. Import/Get Started creates the user's personal instance
> This is the most important Phase 4 transition.
> Viewing the Library must create nothing personal.
> Only when Alice deliberately chooses something like:
> Get Started
> or
> Add to My Decks
>
> does the system establish her personal learning state.
> That should create the appropriate positive personal records:
> - a DeckData record for the Deck;
> - missing CardData records for Cards she does not already have.
> But importantly, importing a Deck does not clone the canonical content.
> Alice is not receiving her own copy of Bob's DeckTemplate and CardTemplates merely by using them.
> She is creating personal state pointing at the canonical identities/versions she is using.
> Card version rule during import
> This is one of the rules we have repeatedly protected from accidental change.
> For each Card:
> If Alice has never used that Card before:
> she starts on its latest published Card version at the time she enters the Deck.
> She does not necessarily adopt whatever cardVersionAtPublish was recorded when the Deck itself was originally published.
> For example:
> Bob publishes Card X v1
> Alice publishes Deck Y containing X
>
> Later:
> Bob publishes Card X v2
>
> Later still:
> Charlie imports Alice's Deck Y
>
> Charlie gets Card X v2.
> The Deck's cardVersionAtPublish: 1 remains historical/provenance information.
> But:
> If Charlie already has CardData for Card X, perhaps because he encountered X through another Deck months ago, we do not silently change his Card version.
> His existing personal CardData wins.
> He can later be offered an explicit Update.
> That means importing a Deck can legitimately result in a user using:
> Deck Y current personal version
> Card A latest
> Card B an older version already in their CardData
> Card C latest
>
> That is not corruption. It follows from Cards being first-class learning identities.
> 4. Library needs to recognize content the user already has
> Although Library itself remains canonical-only, its actions/status should know enough about the user to avoid offering nonsensical choices.
> For example, if Alice sees a public Deck that is already in My Decks, we should not present it as though she has never seen it.
> Conceptually we have discussed statuses/actions such as:
> Get Started      — never imported
> Open             — currently in My Decks
> Restore          — previously archived
> Update available — personal version is behind
>
> I regard the exact wording and exact Phase-4 extent of this UI as something we should confirm during planning rather than silently assume.
> But the architecture already needs to support the distinction.
> Most importantly:
> Archived Deck
> If Alice imported Deck v1, later archived it, and then finds the Deck in Library after public v2 exists:
> Restore means restore her existing personal Deck.
> It must not silently turn restoration into an upgrade.
> So:
> Alice used Deck v1
> Alice archives it
> Bob publishes Deck v2
> Alice encounters Bob's Deck again
> Alice chooses Restore
>
> Alice gets her existing Deck v1 personal state back.
> The UI may tell her that v2 is available, but upgrading is a separate deliberate operation.
> The same principle applies at Card level.
> What Phase 4 is NOT
> I think keeping this boundary strict is important.
> Phase 4 is not yet the full polished Library.
> I would not expect it to solve things like:
> - powerful search;
> - recommendations;
> - categories;
> - ranking;
> - featured creators;
> - sophisticated browsing;
> - moderation/discovery UX;
> - filters;
> - social proof;
> - rich creator profiles.
> That is Phase 7 territory.
> And Phase 4 is not cross-owner editing.
> Alice can consume Bob's public content, but the polished experience where Alice hits Edit and seamlessly creates her own fork belongs to Phase 5.
> Similarly, Phase 4 does not need the full user-facing Deck/Card update adoption system. We need to preserve the architecture and surface enough information to avoid wrong behaviour, but Update itself is primarily a Phase 5 concern.
> How I picture the minimum end-to-end Phase 4 user journey
> The cleanest test of Phase 4 would be two accounts.
> Bob — creator
> Bob creates:
> Card A — public
> Card B — public
> Card C — public
>
> and a Deck using those Cards.
> He publishes the Deck publicly.
> The public publication succeeds only because all three Cards are public.
> Alice — Library visitor
> Alice opens Library.
> She can see Bob's Deck.
> She opens it.
> She sees Bob's canonical public content only.
> Nothing appears in Alice's My Decks merely because she previewed it.
> No CardData is created.
> No DeckData is created.
> No target dates are generated.
> No progress exists.
> Alice chooses Get Started
> Now the system creates Alice's personal DeckData and whatever CardData is missing.
> The Deck appears in My Decks.
> From this point onward, the existing working-Deck machinery takes over.
> Alice's:
> - progress;
> - signals;
> - reflection;
> - personal uploads;
> - chats;
> - tests;
> - target dates
> all live in her personal state rather than contaminating Bob's canonical content.
> Reuse becomes important immediately
> Suppose Alice already has Bob's Card B through another Deck.
> When she imports this Deck, we must reuse Alice's existing CardData for B.
> We do not create a second independent personal CardData merely because another Deck contains the Card.
> That is a core benefit of the first-class Card architecture.
> So if Alice had already:
> - completed Step 1;
> - set confidence signals;
> - written a reflection;
> - uploaded personal material;
> then when B appears through the newly imported Deck, that personal state should still be there.
> Likewise its existing adopted Card version stays intact until Alice deliberately updates it.
> Some implementation-level implications
> Without seeing the current repository, I wouldn't prescribe exact functions/routes/components, but architecturally I would expect Phase 4 to keep three resolution paths quite distinct.
> Canonical Library resolution
> Something conceptually like:
> public Deck root
> → latest public Deck version
> → public canonical Card content
>
> No CardData involved.
> Import transaction
> Something conceptually like:
> validate requested public Deck/version
> ↓
> create or restore DeckData as appropriate
> ↓
> for each Card:
>     existing CardData?
>         yes → preserve it
>         no  → create against latest published Card version
> ↓
> establish personal Deck
>
> This needs to be atomic enough that a partial failure doesn't leave Alice with half an imported Deck.
> Working My Decks resolution
> Then use the personal records:
> DeckData
> + CardData
> + canonical versions those records reference
>
> That should remain distinct from Library resolution.
> Keeping those three paths conceptually separate will prevent a lot of the version/personal-overlay mistakes we've spent the last few phases eliminating.
> Security/privacy boundary Phase 4 will exercise for the first time
> This phase is also where several fixes we've just made actually become important.
> A foreign user must never be able to get to:
> - private Cards merely because a public Deck once referenced something related;
> - private-era Card versions because the Card is public now;
> - private-era Deck versions because the Deck is public now;
> - another user's CardData;
> - another user's chats/tests/uploads/reflections/signals;
> - source personal history from somebody else's forks.
> Public canonical content and personal learning state must remain completely separate.
> That's why I think Phase 4 is a useful architecture checkpoint rather than merely “build a Library page.”
> One area I would want Codex to investigate before we finalize the Phase 4 plan
> There is one thing I would deliberately not turn into a rule from memory alone: exactly what content version a Library Deck preview should display for Cards whose latest Card version is newer than the version recorded in the published Deck.
> We've definitely settled the new entrant adoption rule: new users get the latest published Card version.
> We've also settled that cardVersionAtPublish is historical rather than a permanent adoption pin.
> But there is still a distinction between:
> what the canonical Library preview visually shows
>
> and
> what Card version gets established when the user presses Get Started.
>
> I think the natural result may be that Library shows the latest canonical public Card as well, but before declaring that a locked rule I want Codex to inspect how the current canonical Deck resolution is actually designed and show us the consequences. This is exactly the sort of apparently-small decision that can accidentally collapse our Deck-version/history semantics if we make it casually.
> So when we start the actual Phase 4 planning prompt, I would explicitly ask Codex to investigate that rather than let it choose silently.
> Otherwise, I think the Phase 4 product boundary is now quite clear: publish publicly → canonical-only minimal Library preview → deliberate import → establish/reuse personal DeckData and CardData, while maintaining all of the version/privacy boundaries we've built in Phases 1–3.
